I no longer have the money and the energy to clear the head-high debris from our house,” he says.

The ordeal has been similar or worse for Moromi Bora Bordoloi of Bihubar Siloni Majgaon, Ranjit Gogoi of Charing Gogoi Ali, Pithuram Konwar of Dighalijan, and Jatin Saikia of Bhitoruwal Gaon. “We were just not prepared, maybe because we are not used to such water fury,” Bordoloi, a weaver-homemaker, says.

Caught unaware

The Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat district authorities, too, were caught unawares by the deluge. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, after touring the flood-hit districts, admitted that the administration in each could not mobilise rescue and relief operations for seven days since the disaster struck. He said this was understandable, as these districts do not have a history of major floods and the authorities were not as disaster-ready as other districts that experience floods regularly.

These three districts accounted for 71 of the 99 people who died in the floods across 16 districts from April to August 8, 2026, and more than 94% of some 7.21 lakh flood-affected people. The scale of the disaster across much of the 4,426 sq. km covered by the three districts is perhaps comparable to the 11-day flooding of southern Assam’s Silchar town in June 2022, with water levels rising to 12 feet in some areas. There’s a difference though: Silchar is prone to flooding or water-logging, often fleetingly, unlike Charaideo or Sivasagar.

Disaster management experts explained why the government machinery was underprepared in the three districts. “There’s a flaw in the government’s approach to disaster management, which is to identify risks and concentrate on high-risk areas. The planning needs to change. If low or zero-risk areas become high-risk overnight, there’s very little people can do, as was the case with the three districts,” says Partha Jyoti Das, a climate, water, and disaster specialist with Assam-based biodiversity conservation group Aaranyak. He adds that getting the right people for climate-smart or climate-resilient flood management is crucial. “Ditto with factoring in fluctuating climate change scenarios in everything to minimise disasters.”

According to the 2018 Climate Vulnerability Assessment prepared by the Indian Institute of Technology-Guwahati and IIT-Mandi in collaboration with Bengaluru’s Indian Institute of Science, Assam was the most vulnerable State in the Indian Himalayan region.

The 2021 index of the same assessment ranked Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Bihar as the States most vulnerable to extreme climate events and hydro-meteorological disasters. The index analysed 640 districts in India and found that 463 of these were vulnerable to extreme floods, droughts, and cyclones, and that more than 80% of the country’s population resides in districts highly exposed to climate risks.

Rainfall-induced floods, landslides, and erosion indicate that people in all 35 districts in Assam are highly exposed to climate risks. Often, 25-32 districts experience floods in a year, more severe in districts perched below 88 metres, the average elevation of Sivasagar and Charaideo districts.

This is not unusual. A combination of geography, medium-to-heavy monsoon rainfall for almost six months, and a network of silt-laden rivers has made floods an annual phenomenon in Assam.

Experts say the pattern of flooding changed after the Assam-Tibet earthquake in 1950 triggered massive landslides across the eastern Himalayas, sending large volumes of sediment into the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries and permanently altering the river system.

Deforestation (Assam lost about 3,600 sq. km of tree cover from 2001–2025, accelerating soil erosion and making the rivers shallower with silt), infrastructure push in the geologically young and fragile hills, ageing breach-prone river embankments, and climate change amplified the recurring disaster, often suddenly in specific areas instead of the “laahe-laahe (slow) flooding” of yore.

Hydrologists and disaster specialists are baffled by the ever-changing rainfall pattern, drenching some areas heavily and barely wetting others. For instance, while Sivasagar and Charaideo districts drowned, their western neighbours, the perennially flood-prone Morigaon and Nagaon districts, faced drought-like situations. This, perhaps, explains the monsoon paradox.

According to the India Meteorological Department, Assam recorded a 28% rainfall deficit in June and July, while about 6,500 sq. km area on either side of the Assam-Nagaland border received up to 490% more rainfall than normal, contributing to the floods in Sivasagar and Charaideo.

Mining menace

When India’s National Green Tribunal banned Meghalaya’s hazardous rat-hole coal mining in April 2014, green activists in Assam sought attention to similar, potentially “more dangerous” activities along the State’s borders with Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. More than a decade ago, Golaghat-based activist Apurba Ballav Goswami said the water bodies in Assam linked to the Nagaland-origin Dikhow, Disang, Jhanji, and Teyap Rivers were turning acidic due to run-off from unscientifically established mines. This, he said, was foreboding for downstream areas in Assam.

A 2018 PIL (public interest litigation) filed by Congress leader Debabarata Saikia, then a Congress MLA from Nazira, in the Gauhati High Court indicated rampant coal mining was not the only source of disaster for Sivasagar and adjoining districts. It conveyed that illegal sand and stone mining and encroachment of fragile river beds were also inviting trouble. The PIL focussed on the Dikhow, Sivasagar’s lifeline-turned-sorrow, seeking an immediate ban on the potentially catastrophic riverbed mining.

Following the court’s directive, the government sent teams from January to March 2019 to verify the allegations, concentrating on Bihubar and adjoining areas near the Assam-Nagaland border. The inquiry revealed eight stone quarries, 81 stone crushers, and the seizure of about 10,000 cubic metres of minor minerals in the area. The report described Bihubar and the surrounding areas as a hub of mining, distribution, supply, and interstate transportation. It also said that most of the gravel and boulders were transported from Nagaland.

Saikia petitioned the High Court again in 2019, arguing that illegal mining was continuing despite the damning government report, which the court had reproduced in its order. The second petition sought a specialised mining task force, a high-powered committee to study the fragile ecosystem of the Dikhow, measures to prevent changes in the river’s course, and a master plan covering illegal mining, bank erosion, drainage, and associated problems.

In October 2019, the court directed the Assam government to constitute a dedicated Mines and Minerals Task Force Battalion and a high-level committee for river conservation, adding that it expected action within three months.

“The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government virtually ignored the directive. Unchecked stone and sand mining in the Dikhow contributed to the extensive soil erosion along its course from Nagaland. The outcome is the ordeal our district went through in July,” Saikia, from oil town Nazira near Sivasagar, says. Nazira is the Assam Asset’s headquarters of ONGC, whose office-residential complex was submerged, forcing many executives to stay in hotels and homestays on higher ground.

Sivasagar MLA and Raijor Dal president Akhil Gogoi was more vocal about the “indiscriminate” coal and stone mining. “Rainwater accumulated in the hollowed coal pits in Nagaland, eventually burst out and caused widespread devastation in Assam,” he says, also pointing to the “rape of the rivers” by the mining mafia. His Sivasagar-based party leader Manas Konwar went a step further, naming two local BJP legislators, one of them a Minister, as the kingpins of the stone and coal mining operations along the Assam-Nagaland border.

After the floods, local YouTubers and reel-makers filmed the mining activities along the border. Some of them showed several earthen roads built across the Dikhow River to facilitate the movement of trucks carrying coal, stone chips, and sand. “Built during the dry season, these roads are like multiple dams that block the water upstream, within Nagaland. The accumulated water swells during the monsoon and cuts through these dams,” a Brahmaputra Board official says, declining to be quoted. The primary role of this Board, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, is to plan, coordinate, and integrate implementation of measures to control floods, mitigate riverbank erosion, and harness water resources across the northeastern region.

While the Assam Chief Minister, speaking to the media, denied any mining activities in Assam, community-based organisations in Nagaland rejected “theories” that their hill State and their people were responsible for Assam’s floods.

Former Nagaland minister Mmhonlumo Kikon noted reports that Nagaland’s insurgent groups are financially involved in coal mining, and that mining in Nagaland materially caused or intensified the eastern Assam floods. He also said the reports frequently move from allegations, anecdotes, and general environmental risks to an implied conclusion about criminality and flood causation without producing the evidence needed to make that connection. “A clear and thorough report on the investors from Assam or elsewhere, the market where this coal is sold, the number of challans (invoices) issued by the relevant departments in Assam, or even the Assam police record on the trucks transporting the coal would have been helpful,” he says.

Post-flood trauma

Sivasagar was formerly known as Rangpur, the administrative and political capital of the Ahoms, who ruled large swathes of Assam for 600 years until the British took control of the region in the early 1800s. Historians say Sivasagar (Charaideo was carved out of it in August 2015) was strategic for the Ahoms to administer a vast region, and that the region was relatively flood-free compared to the rest of the Brahmaputra Valley. The Ahom royal chronicles refer to flooding in and around the capital at intervals of more than a hundred years, including in 1691 and 1793.

“Sivasagar’s misery indicates that the flood cycle may have reduced (after the last one recorded 60 years ago) and become more catastrophic due to several factors, mostly man-made. The unpredictable climate change scenario is adding to this misery, making old water discharge data on which flood control measures are designed redundant,” says Bibhash Sarma, an engineering teacher and consultant to Assam’s Water Resources Department.

Aaranyak’s Das adds that the ever-changing rainfall pattern is the new normal. “The administrative machinery must understand that no part of Assam or anywhere else in the northeast is safe from floods and associated disasters. Everyone, down to the farmer, needs to be wired to anticipate such calamities during the six rainy months in the region.”

According to disaster watchers, getting the right people for climate-smart or climate-resilient flood management will not be enough to reduce disasters in a State where living with “normal” floods has been a way of life. “Disaster preparedness has to be designed around the realisation that there is not an inch of flood-free land in Assam, and that areas considered zero- or low-risk can become high-risk overnight,” Das says. Others called for surface water management by undoing or minimising the damage done by unscientifically planned roads, flyovers, hydropower, housing, and other infrastructure projects, which have largely claimed wetlands that once acted as water sponges during floods.

The pessimism “unless corrective measures are initiated now” has sunk in among Sivasagar-Charaideo’s flood survivors. Neighbours joked about taking refuge in her house during extreme floods when Lakshmi Devi began constructing her RCC house at Bihubar Nepalikhuti in 2022.

In 2026, more than 60 of them did take refuge on the roof of her house when the “tsunami” struck the village on July 19. “I could not imagine then that the joke would become a reality in less than four years,” she says, mourning the loss of her 10 cows. “I may have to add another floor to our house, but there’s no guarantee that the next flood will not reach the second-floor ceiling,” she adds.

District officials say the challenges in the areas returning to normality include clearing several feet of silt and debris from houses and paddy fields, sanitising the foul-smelling flood-hit areas, and ensuring adequate healthcare for livestock and people vulnerable to water- and vector-borne diseases such as Japanese encephalitis, which claimed 19 lives this year, before the floods.

The biggest challenge could be the trauma of expecting the worst in a State that recorded 160 and 181 human deaths during the 2017 and 2022 floods, respectively. “I don’t think anyone in Jorhat, Sivasagar, or Charaideo can sleep peacefully, at least during the remaining two months of the monsoon this year, if not later,” says Sarmah, whose Tamuli Gaon village is 18 km south of the Brahmaputra. “The Brahmaputra has been a bigger sorrow for Assam than the Dikhow this time, and much closer to us,” he says.

rahul.karmakar@thehindu.co.in

World.title: West Asia war updates: Netanyahu vows Iran will 'not have nuclear weapons' with or without deal
World.content:
This liveblog is now closed.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday (August 9, 2026) they would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz, vital to the world economy, until the United States met Tehran’s conditions set out the day before, including compensation for war damages.

Also Read: Mecca Agreement | A new triple alliance in West Asia

Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the United States and Israel attacked in late February, and wants to charge tolls for passage, striking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

Meanwhile, the UAE accused Iran on Saturday (August 8, 2026) of targeting a tanker belonging to its state-owned oil company in the Strait of Hormuz, even as both Iran and Oman suggested talks on administering the vital waterway were progressing. Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

Also Read: U.S. expects deal soon on Strait of Hormuz

Iran’s politburo-like body, known as the Supreme National Security Council, said the Strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour,” issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway and traffic on it.

World.title: Russia says it captures two villages in eastern Ukraine, Kyiv reports frontline battles
World.content:
Russian forces have taken ​control of the two villages in Ukraine’s eastern ‌Donetsk region, state-run RIA news agency reported ​on Sunday (August 9, 2026), citing the Russian ⁠Defence Ministry.

The ministry report on Telegram said Russian forces had seized Vasyutinske, a few kilometers east of ‌the “fortress city” of Kramatorsk, and Toretsk, southwest of the city of ‌Druzhkivka.

Ukrainian forces made no acknowledgement of ‌the ⁠two settlements changing hands and Reuters ⁠could not verify the battlefield reports independently.

Russia is slowly advancing westward through Donetsk region, though there has been ​little significant change ‌for months in the positions along the 1,200-km (775-mile) frontline.

The Ukrainian war blog DeepState, which uses open source reports in documenting ‌the frontline positions of both sides, reported ​that Russian forces had made advances near Illinivka -- outside the contested city ⁠of Kostiantynivka.

It also reported Russian advances near Chasiv Yar, to the west of the ‌city of Bakhmut, which fell to Russian forces in 2023 after long months of heavy fighting.

The Ukrainian military’s General Staff, in a late evening report, said Kyiv’s forces had repelled 24 attacks ‌around Kostiantynivka, Illinivka and other centres.

Russian commanders said last ​month their forces had seized Kostiantynivka, but Ukrainian officials have disputed the ⁠claim.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in his nightly ⁠video address on Sunday made no reference to changes in frontline positions, but ‌singled out for praise Ukrainian forces fighting in specific areas, notably Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka ​and Kramatorsk.

World.title: Trump announces staff secretary Will Scharf will be his new White House counsel
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday (August 9, 2026) that his new White House counsel will be Will Scharf, the staff secretary who as the Trump-appointed head of the National Capital Planning Commission helped secure approval for the $400 million ballroom project.

Mr. Trump said that, beginning September 1, Mr. Scharf will be replacing David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Mr. Trump noted that Mr. Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the Supreme Court.

“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”

The shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture — just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Mr. Trump’s Republican Party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Mr. Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.

The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the Justice Department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.

Mr. Trump in July 2025 had named Mr. Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.

Mr. Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled on Friday (August 7, 2026) that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Mr. Trump has vowed to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.

World.title: Several injured in Denmark in suspected underworld shooting: police
World.content:
Several people were wounded on Sunday (August 9, 2026) in a shooting in Denmark that police believed was linked to a settling of scores among criminals.

Police said in a statement they were present at several locations in Holbaek, about 70 km west of Copenhagen, following "a shooting in which multiple people have been hit".

The incident was reported to police around 3:45 p.m. (1345 GMT).

"At this time, we cannot provide further information about their condition. The police presumption is that this is a settling of scores within the criminal milieu."

The perpetrators were seen leaving the scene in a white car, according to preliminary information, police said, asking members of the public with information to come forward.

World.title: Israeli military closes Palestinian Christian village Taybeh, citing settler attacks
World.content:
Israel’s military on Sunday (August 9, 2026) closed the West Bank village ​of Taybeh to non-residents, saying it aimed to prevent growing ‌attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers across the West ​Bank.

The order, the military said, only ⁠applies to Israelis and not to Palestinians. A spokesperson said turning Taybeh into a closed military zone was “due to some violent attacks ‌by Israelis in the region.”

“Upon receiving any report of violations of the order, IDF soldiers are dispatched ‌to the area and operate to disperse the gatherings ‌and ⁠detain suspects in order to protect the ⁠citizens of the area and to maintain order,” the military said in a statement.

Taybeh is one of the only Christian villages remaining in the ​West Bank and was ‌visited last year by the Greek Orthodox patriarch and the Roman Catholic cardinal of Jerusalem.

It is also home to the Taybeh Brewing Co, widely considered West Asia’s oldest microbrewery.

Some Western countries have announced sanctions ​on settler groups over violent Israeli attacks on Palestinians.

In June, Israeli settlers obstructed Palestinians putting out ⁠a large blaze near Taybeh in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian civil defence firefighters and a local priest ‌who described an “ongoing pattern of intimidation and unjustified violence” that undermined the residents’ fundamental rights.

A U.N. inquiry released on Tuesday (August 4, 2026) found that Israeli authorities were directly involved in settler attacks that have killed, injured and displaced Palestinians in the West Bank. The Israeli mission in Geneva rejected the ‌report’s findings, saying Israeli authorities including the president and prime minister had ​repeatedly condemned violence against Palestinians.

Parts of Taybeh are located in Area B, where the Palestinian Authority ⁠runs civil administration but where security control must be coordinated ⁠with Israeli authorities.

The West Bank and Jerusalem are home to around 50,000 Palestinian Christians, members of ‌a religious community there stretching back to antiquity in a region that is home to many of the ​faith’s most important holy sites.

World.title: Pushing One Health approach, U.P. priorities early identification and reporting of emerging zoonotic diseases
World.content:
Uttar Pradesh Animal Husbandry department on Sunday (August 9, 2026) said it is strengthening the capacity for early identification and reporting of emerging zoonotic diseases, surveillance systems, laboratory strengthening, outbreak preparedness, pushing the One Health approach framework.

“Recently, the Animal Husbandry Department developed a Compendium for Veterinarians on Zoonotic & Priority Animal Diseases,. The compendium has been designed to strengthen the knowledge of field veterinarians on priority zoonotic diseases, standardized case definitions, surveillance and timely disease reporting. We are strengthening the capacity for early identification and reporting of priority zoonotic and other important animal diseases. The state will also enhance its diagnostic capacity through ELISA-based testing for priority zoonotic diseases. Interventions to strengthen farm-level biosecurity in Pilibhit and Gorakhpur districts, promoting improved disease prevention and infection control practices, is also taking place. The State is committed to strengthen One Health systems through coordinated interdepartmental action,” told Mukesh Kumar Meshram, Additional Chief Secretary, Animal Husbandry, Dairy Development and Fisheries Department, to The Hindu.

Mr. Meshram, a 1995-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer said that under the RISE Global Health Security (RISE GHS) Project, the Animal Husbandry Department, in collaboration with the Forest and Wildlife Department, successfully conducted active surveillance for Avian Influenza among wild migratory birds at 19 Ramsar and other important wetland sites across Uttar Pradesh.

“During the previous migratory season, over 1,100 samples were collected and tested at IVRI, Bareilly. Building on this success, similar surveillance will be undertaken during the upcoming migratory bird season across all Ramsar sites and other important wetlands in the state. A State-Level Training of Trainers (ToT) programme for government veterinarians will be conducted to strengthening One Health systems through coordinated interdepartmental action. We are focused on emerging zoonotic threats, spillover risks and multisectoral strategies for disease prevention, while the second deliberated on strengthening One Health surveillance through early detection, integrated data sharing and coordinated outbreak response,” he added.

World.title: Maharashtra FDA to introduce end-to-end traceability of milk to fight adulteration
World.content:
In a bid to arrest the frequent and recurring incidents of milk adulteration in Maharashtra, the State’s Food and Drug Administration has planned a massive digitisation initiative for end-to-end traceability of milk. The project intends to digitise milking records and link them to the milch animals, thereby helping authorities monitor real milk output. The initiative is in its nascent stage and will be rolled out once the project report for digitisation of milking records is completed, Maharashtra FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe told The Hindu.

“We have started a project to start a portal. All the milk collection centres will have to upload their data on that portal. The portal will be made, managed and monitored by the FDA. We will have access to this data and the data of the milch animals in that region which is uploaded on NDLM. This data will be available at the back-end. It won’t be available to front-end users,” he said during an interview.

Maharashtra FDA has, over the last few months, cracked down against milk adulteration, has banned analogue paneer in the State for a year, has banned the sale of junk foods in and around schools. The FDA has conducted large number of raids across the State on restaurants, eateries, caterers’ outlets. It has also increased its testing capacity. The moves have led to some litigations too, with a few establishments claiming the action to be harsh and ‘not in adherence to the legal provisions’.

At present, it is mandatory for milk collection centres and dairies to maintain data about the milk which is accepted, and that which is rejected. “As FDA, we plan to launch a portal where the dairies will have to update this real time data on the portal. The NDLM (National Digital Livestock Mission) already has the data about milch animals. We also know the average milk output of the animals, as the farmer uploads the data on the portal. We will match the database from both these portals at the back-end. This data will not be available to the dairies or at the front end. This will help us understand and catch adulteration,” he said.

The FDA is currently in the process of preparing a project report for the digitisation bid. “The report will be submitted in a few months’ time. But, for the project to go live will take some time. It will have to be developed, tested,” he said.

“The biggest challenge for us is tracing milk to the milch animal. Unless we can do that, we will not be able to completely annihilate adulteration. It will continue to be done at a large scale. Is it possible to trace milk to milch animals? Yes. It has been done across the world,” he said while answering questions about the feasibility of the project.

Explaining the process, he said that the FDA will take help of the National Digital Livestock Mission (NDLM) database. It is a digital initiative by the Government of India to manage livestock data. “In India, there is an animal tagging system in which the animal is tagged and identified. Whether it is milch animal or not, has to be updated by the farmer. this will help us understand milk production to milk consumption in totality,” he said.

Why is Tukaram Mundhe on a mission to put clean food on our plates? | Pulse Maharashtra

How adulteration happens

Explaining the systemic issues which lead to milk adulteration, he said, “When the farmer milks the animal, the milk has to reach the chilling centre within two hours. Once the milk is stored without chilling beyond two hours, its acidity increases. To neutralise that, adulteration starts. It is a practice that milk dairies collect only once in a day. Then what happens to the milk which is milked at night? That is how the role of neutraliser comes in and adulteration begins. To increase quality and quantity, water is added. To increase the fat content, other things are added. We need to break that cycle. If the milk is not collected at night, then it crosses the two-hour window. That is when the farmer is forced to do something about it,” he said.

In July, Maharashtra FDA issued a compliance order, asking dairies to collect milk before 8 a.m.

The FDA also wants dairies to collect milk twice. Lack of availability of sufficient chilling centres is another challenge which needs immediate address. “Once milk is chilled at less than 4°C within two hours of collection, it is safe. There is no need to add anything,” he said.

World.title: Pak-Saudi-Turkiye defence pact open to any other country in region, 'purely defensive': DPM Dar
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister said on Sunday that the defence pact signed between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye remained “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles.

He also clarified that the agreement was “purely defensive” in nature.

The indication that an expansion of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed in the Saudi city on Friday, was possible came a day after the Turkish foreign minister said Egypt could be joining the pact.

The pact aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

Dar further elaborated on the pact, which he referred to as the Makkah Accord, in a post on X.

“The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement […] reflects the depth of the brotherly relations between the leadership and peoples of the three countries.

“The Makkah Accord is the culmination of years of discussions and coordination, with a common desire to strengthen strategic cooperation in addressing multifarious peace and security challenges and advancing regional peace, stability and prosperity,” he said.

He clarified that the pact did not abrogate or replace any existing bilateral or multilateral agreements between the signatory countries, or with other countries or organisations.

Reiterating that any external armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all under the pact, he said it was consistent with the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

Moreover, he said, the accord was “purely defensive” in nature.

“It is not targeted against any country and its sole purpose is to further strengthen our ongoing efforts towards peace, stability and prosperity in the wider region.”

“The Makkah Accord remains open to any country in the region willing to uphold its fundamental principles and resolve differences through mutual respect, cooperation and peaceful means,” he said, adding that the pact was consistent with the fundamental pillars of Islamabad’s foreign policy.

“Pakistan looks forward to continuing to work closely with all brotherly countries in the region towards lasting peace and stability. We remain committed to advancing the cause of peaceful resolution of all conflicts and building a more secure, stable and prosperous future for our peoples,” he concluded.

Later in the day, Dar and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand exchanged views on the regional situation, including the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

Dar informed Anand of the “essence of the agreement and the joint resolve of the three countries to contribute to regional peace, stability and security”.

Egypt likely to join: Turkish FM

Earlier, on Saturday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also said he believed Egypt could join the pact once several technical issues were resolved.

“Egypt is already our natural partner on all issues. I believe that at the next stage, Egypt will also be among us in the alliance. We already act toward one another as if we were alliance members. There are a few technical issues. Once these are implemented, there is no reason for Egypt not to be part of it,” he told Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu news agency.

Other countries had expressed interest in joining the agreement, but the founding members had debated how the expansion should be handled, he further stated.

Some countries that wanted to join asked not to be named, he said, adding that the preferred model was for Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to remain the three core founding countries, responsible for establishing the principles, standards and long-term structure of the alliance, while other countries could join with the approval of the core members.

“Under our president’s vision, we should not remain limited to three countries. We should grow,” Fidan said.

Fidan also said the initiative was broader than the traditional definition of the Middle East because of Pakistan’s participation.

Pakistan’s geographical position meant the initiative went beyond the conventional definition of the Middle East and represented a broader regional perspective.

‘Same as Nato’s Article 5’

Fidan further elaborated on this, saying the pact was technically the same as Nato’s Article 5 mutual defence agreement.

Article 5 of the North Atlantic alliance specifies that an attack on one ​of its members is an attack on all of them. It obliges allies to take action they deem necessary to assist the country under attack, including potentially the use of military force.

While the Makkah defence pact stipulates the same, Fidan explained that its text contained general commitments whose practical implementation would depend on discussions and decisions by relevant bodies.

A country would need to make a request for assistance and would determine the type of support it needs, he said, adding that the requests could be of different kinds, ranging from intelligence and logistics to ammunition or, if necessary, military units, depending on the scale of the threat.

The signatories, he said, would decide through consultations what degree, form, and format of ​support they would ask for in the event of an attack, but that no country would be considered a ​threat as long as a member state is not attacked.

Fidan also said that the new alliance was not directed against Iran or any other country, but rather served as a general pledge to support the three signatories’ security.

He further told Anadolu that discussions on the initiative began before the current war environment, when there was no US-Israel war on Iran and other regional countries had also been involved in the talks leading to the agreement.

Fidan said its signatories were countries that did not have expansionist policies. “They are countries concerned with their own borders, their own problems and their development, and, if possible, they want to contribute positively to their environment through good relations and good neighbourliness.“

The three countries, he said, had different styles and capacities, but when brought together, they naturally formed a defence-oriented organisation rather than an offensive one.

“It is not an approach of going on the offensive and saying, ‘Let’s do this or that together.’ Therefore, unless it is attacked by a country, whether from inside or outside the region, this alliance cannot have any dispute with any country. But, of course, the power composition we have put forward will make a constructive contribution to regional stability,” he said.

He termed the pact the “most important step” toward bringing lasting stability to this region.

How will the alliance function?

According to Fidan, the pact would be operational under a political and military committee comprising foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of general staff, similar to Nato structures.

The committee would translate the vision set by the leaders into decisions and carry out related work, while a secretariat would be established to implement those decisions, he explained.

“At the first committee meeting, ministers would likely present proposals to the leaders on the establishment, structure and functioning of the secretariat, as well as its initial tasks,” he said, adding that the pact would cover a broad range of military issues, including interoperability, or the ability of countries with different military structures to operate together. Other areas would include joint training, mutual support, logistics, threat assessments, intelligence sharing and, most importantly, defence industry cooperation.

He said the committee would meet at certain intervals during the year and that a permanent secretariat would be established in Saudi Arabia. The structure, functioning and additional units of the secretariat would be determined in discussions among the members.

Fidan added that joint exercises and training would be necessary to establish the ability of the countries to operate together.

“Because after a while you will see that when you find yourselves in a common combat scenario, how your weapons systems and communications systems will communicate with one another and how they will be compatible are important issues. These are the things that will be done after the secretariat is established,” he said.

He said standards would need to be developed and that analyses and assessments would also be carried out.

‘Support in the Muslim world and the West’

Fidan said the defence agreement had received strong support from countries in the Muslim world, including those that were not members but were nevertheless very pleased with the agreement.

He said there were also supporters in the West who understood the substance of the initiative.

“Especially in the Islamic world, there are many who strongly support this issue. There are also supporters in the West, among those who understand the essence of the matter. The way for the Middle East to cease being a place that produces problems for humanity and the international community and instead become a place that creates added value with everything it possesses is through implementing constructive alliances of this kind,” Fidan said.

Fidan said the leadership of Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had created significant regional and global expectations and that officials now had the responsibility to fill those expectations professionally.

“Our responsibility, in the positions we hold, is to recognise that the political will put forward by the leadership of the three countries has created a very significant regional and global expectation. We need to fill that expectation very professionally, move forward step by step and make it work. We have begun doing this, and God willing, we will continue,” he said.

The signing of the accord comes at a time of heightened regional tensions, with Pakistan seeking to balance ties with Middle Eastern and Western partners.

Analysts say many in the region view the development as a step toward Gulf states taking greater responsibility for their own security.

Israel’s increasingly aggressive military posture in recent years has also emerged as an important factor shaping how Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye perceive the regional security environment, they added.

For decades, Saudi Arabia has relied heavily on its strategic relationship with the United States for its security. Experts note the new agreement does not replace Washington, but it does create an additional security pillar.

“The regional states are not seeking to sever ties with Washington, but neither do they want to entrust their security exclusively to American guarantees,” one analyst said.

Additional input from Syed Irfan Raza

World.title: Sindh govt decides judicial commission to probe Mir Raza Ali murder case
World.content:
KARACHI: The Sindh government has decided to seek a judicial probe into the killing of 25-year-old businessman Mir Raza Ali, Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar said on Sunday.

Ali’s body was found in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he went missing on July 28. While his family is convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, police had previously been building the case around the possibility that he died by suicide.

However, after injury details from a second postmortem ruled out the possibility of suicide, a murder charge was added to the case on Sunday.

“A decision has been taken to conduct a judicial inquiry into the murder case of Mir Raza Ali Khan,” the Sindh home minister said in a statement issued by his office.

According to the statement, Lanjar, along with Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab, visited Ali’s residence to meet his parents. They assured the family that they would be provided complete justice.

Lanjar said the judicial commission would be constituted under the leadership of a Sindh High Court judge on the recommendation of the Sindh chief minister.

During the meeting, Lanjar briefed Ali’s parents in detail about the progress of the case and the investigation, the statement said.

“The investigation team will maintain full contact and cooperation with the deceased’s parents,” the minister was quoted as saying. “A transparent and impartial investigation into the case will be ensured.”

He affirmed that all requirements of justice would be fulfilled and no leniency would be shown to anyone responsible.

Meanwhile, the Karachi mayor noted that Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah chaired a four-hour-long meeting during which “all aspects of the incident and the investigation were reviewed in detail”.

The decision of a judicial inquiry comes after Faryal Talpur, the chairperson of Sindh Assembly’s Standing Committee on Home, recommended that CM Murad constitute a judicial commission for a “transparent, impartial and comprehensive investigation” into the case.

Taking notice of Ali’s murder, she said the proposed commission should examine all aspects of the incident and bring the facts to light.

“Legal and disciplinary action should be taken without discrimination against those found responsible in light of the commission’s findings,” Talpur added.

She further stressed that justice for the victim’s family must be ensured at all costs and that the public should be transparently informed of all facts surrounding the case.

“No negligence or bias will be tolerated in meeting the requirements of justice,” she said, adding that providing justice to the bereaved family and maintaining public confidence in the justice system were fundamental responsibilities of the government and relevant institutions.

Probe handed to Zaman Town police; 2 officers suspended

In another development, Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town Police Station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered.

According to a statement by the police spokesperson, the investigation of the case has now been entrusted to SIO/Inspector Chaudhry Ghazanfar Ali of Zaman Town Police Station.

“Under the order, Inspector Ghazanfar will complete the investigation under the supervision of the investigation team constituted by the Sindh IG,” the statement said.

“The Karachi additional IG has directed that the investigation be completed in accordance with the requirements of justice, transparency and law, and that the report be submitted to the relevant court,” it added.

Moreover, the additional IG also ordered the immediate suspension of Sharea Faisal sub-divisional police officer (SDPO) Muhammad Arshad Afridi and Gulistan-i-Jauhar Station House Officer (SHO) Kamran Qureshi.

They were suspended over “failure to preserve the crime scene and carry out proper crime scene investigation”, AIG Khan told Dawn.

According to a statement released by the police spokesperson, the AIG also ordered SHO Qureshi’s reversion to a lower rank.

“The full implementation of rules, regulations and accountability principles in departmental affairs would be ensured,” the statement said.

“Action will be taken in accordance with the law and rules in case of any violation of discipline by an officer.”

New police team for probe

Earlier on Sunday, an order released by the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death.

It also showed that the murder charge had been added to the first information report (FIR) on his father’s complaint.

The order, seen by Dawn, said the new investigating team was formed in light of Ali’s second postmortem report, which contradicted the one released after his first postmortem, to “supervise the investigation of FIR no. 795/2026 u/s 365/ 302/ 201 of the PPC”.

Initially, the FIR was registered only under Section 365 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), which pertains to kidnapping.

Of the newly added provisions, Section 302 pertains to murder and Section 201 to hiding the evidence of an offence or giving false information to screen the offender.

The case would now be probed by a five-member team led by Sindh Deputy IG (Crime and Investigation) Amir Farooqui and comprising Rapid Response Force Al-Falah SSP Syed Muhammad Ali Raza, Korangi SP (Investigation) Qais Khan, Central SP (Investigation) Anam Tajjamul and Zaman Town SIO Ch. Ghazanfar, the police order said.

It added: “The team shall undertake a comprehensive and impartial investigation into the case from all relevant angles. The team shall identify, collect, preserve and examine any new or additional evidence and shall thoroughly examine and analyse all physical, technical, circumstantial and forensic evidence collected during the investigation.

“The team shall make all out efforts to work out the case and submit a report to the court concerned within the stipulated period. The team may co-opt any officer to assist in the investigation. Progress shall be reported on a day-to-day basis.”

On Saturday, the lawyer for Ali’s family, Jibran Nasir, had demanded that the first investigation probing the case be replaced, after a fresh post-mortem examination conducted following the exhumation of Ali’s body found that he had been shot in the back — evidence that ruled out the possibility of suicide.

Speaking to the media, he reiterated the allegation that Ali had been tortured before being murdered.

“This was murder following torture — the murder of a happy, ambitious and educated young man from Karachi,” he alleged.

The family’s lawyer also criticised senior police officials, alleging that they “do not want to investigate, but rather humiliate, harass and exhaust the family”.

Advocate Nasir added that he and the family had “no faith” in the investigation team and that they wanted the entire team changed.

Controversy over autopsy

Ali, an Institute of Business Administration graduate and the owner of eatery Wafflix, had gone missing on July 28. The 25-year-old’s body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar.

The latest developments in his case follow a controversy between the Karachi police surgeon and investigators over alleged loopholes in the medico-legal report regarding Ali’s first post-mortem examination.

Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed told a private news channel on Tuesday that the post-mortem findings of Ali’s body had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs.

The police surgeon, whose assessment was based only on the post-mortem report and photographs as she had not examined the body herself back then, had said the reported entry wound, bullet trajectory and exit wound did not correspond with one another.

The police surgeon noted that entry wounds were typically smaller than exit wounds in firearm cases. She also said that gunshot residue, commonly found on the hands in suspected suicides, was not tested for in this case.

Her interview prompted the police authorities to issue a statement, terming such observations as having the potential to adversely affect the ongoing investigation.

The statement, however, said that exhumation of the dead body could be done on the medical board’s recommendation for further clarification by a committee of medico-legal experts with the court’s permission.

On Thursday, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Ali’s father, Mir Hussain Ali, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation.

The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with Dr Syed as the convener. Prof Dr Naseem Ahmed of Dow University of Health Sciences, Dr Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Amir Hassan Khan of Citizens Police Liaison Committee, Additional Police Surgeon Dr Sirichand, Dr Kamran Khan and Dr Daniyal Mirza of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre, and Dr Mohammed Yaseen, the admin in-charge of the police surgeon office, were the other members of the board.

However, in the early hours of Friday, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department.

While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed to Prof Dr Zakiuddin from DUHS, Prof Dr Kazi Akbar and Prof Dr Abid Hussain Chang from Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences, and Hyderabad Police Surgeon Dr Waseem Khan.

On Friday morning, Ali’s family was present at the Tariq Road graveyard for the exhumation, which was deferred after they objected ti the new board. Standing alongside Ali’s father, Nasir had accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts and held the police, health department and the Sindh government responsible for the delay.

The Sindh government then restored the original medical board on Friday, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on Saturday.

After a second postmortem of the body, Dr Syed told Dawn, “We have collected samples for identification, chemical analysis and gunshot residue. The cause of death is reserved for laboratory reports.”

Regarding the autopsy, she said that multiple injuries were found on the head and face. “Fractured rib on the back, which is the entry wound of the gunshot [that] exited from the front,” she said.

She said the body bore “injuries in right flank and feet [and] congealed black substance present in mouth and throat”.

World.title: Pakistan to partner with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar on oil storage scheme
World.content:
Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik on Sunday said plans were underway to launch a scheme with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar for oil storage to strengthen energy security.

Pakistan has been planning to boost domestic storage for crude oil and refined products to increase its energy security, it emerged in May. With no strategic petroleum reserves, the country has been left exposed to oil supply shocks resulting from the US-Iran war that has choked supplies through the Strait of Hormuz .

Addressing a press conference in Lahore today, Malik said: “I am grateful to the governments of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar that we will have a bonded scheme with them, under which these countries will store their oil on the secure territories of Pakistan at their own cost, and supply to the entire world from here.”

He added that Pakistan will have the right that in the case of a conflict, it could “buy those resources from them by paying for them and fulfil our needs”.

The minister said the “commercial bonded scheme drafted with the help of Aramco and other major companies” has been forwarded to the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) upon the directives of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

“When, God-willing, a decision is made on it next week, you will see the progress,” he added, asserting that Pakistan’s energy needs will be fulfilled “without spending money and despite a lack of resources”.

The US-Israel war on Iran has caused oil supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively blockaded, leading to unprecedented hikes in petroleum prices.

The minister said the government was committed to strengthening energy security. He noted that $500 million were required for storing crude oil reserves for one month, in addition to $300-400m needed for an underground storage system.

He said the government would later debate whether the country could invest this amount, adding that the leadership would work on it in the upcoming months.

Highlighting Pakistan’s energy challenges, Malik said the country imported around 90 per cent of its energy requirements, while domestic oil production stood at approximately 70,000 barrels per day against a daily demand of around 500,000 barrels.

He stressed the need to accelerate indigenous oil and gas exploration to reduce reliance on imports.

He said the prime minister and the field marshal had tasked a leading international company with preparing a comprehensive roadmap for the country’s energy sector, which would be presented to the national leadership in the coming months.

Malik also said Turkiye’s Turkish Petroleum would soon commence offshore drilling operations in Pakistan’s territorial waters, paving the way for significant foreign investment in the energy sector.

He announced that tenders for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) would open on Monday and said the government had made arrangements to issue new gas connections to facilitate consumers.

Speaking on international developments, Malik said that despite economic pressures from the US-Iran war, the government ensured uninterrupted fuel supplies across the country and made “every effort” to protect consumers from the full impact of rising global prices.

The minister said the government remained committed to providing maximum relief to the public despite limited financial resources.

He added that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had introduced a transparent petroleum pricing mechanism, with all pricing calculations available on the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority’s (Ogra) website.

Since mid-July, the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices as hostilities between the US and Iran renewed. Before that, petroleum prices were revised weekly since the war began, alongside measures for conserving fuel.

Recalling that the federal cabinet had approved a refinery policy last month, Malik affirmed that the government was resolving long-standing financial issues facing the petroleum sector.

He added that the flow of circular debt had been halted and efforts were underway to clear outstanding liabilities inherited from previous administrations.

World.title: Movement restricted under Section 144 in some areas of South Waziristan, Tank on Monday
World.content:
SOUTH WAZIRISTAN: The administrations of Lower South Waziristan, Upper South Waziristan and Tank have imposed Section 144 in several areas of the three districts for August 10 (Monday), citing security concerns and directing residents to avoid unnecessary movement during the specified hours.

Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) is a legal provision that empowers district administrations to prohibit an assembly of four or more people in an area for a limited period.

The deputy commissioners (DCs) of the three districts issued separate notifications on Sunday evening, imposing restrictions on movement between 6am and 7pm, as well as ordering the closure of markets and business centres in the specified areas.

The administrations of Upper and Lower South Waziristan have also directed motorists to stop their vehicles at least 50 metres before reaching security personnel and for all passengers to get out of the vehicles.

They warned that unauthorised movement or violation of the restrictions would invite action under the law.

According to the notification issued by the Lower South Waziristan administration, a curfew will remain in force in Wana tehsil from 6am to 7pm on Monday. During the curfew, all kinds of movement will remain prohibited, and markets and business centres in certain areas will remain closed.

DC Musarrat Zaman said several important roads and connecting routes in and around Wana would also remain closed to general traffic during the restrictions.

The affected routes include the road from Wana through Tiarza Gate, Karb Kot, Tanai and Azizabad Chowk up to Dargai Bridge. The route from Gul Kuch through Toi Khullah to Tanai has also been included in the restricted areas.

The administration said movement on the affected routes would only be allowed in an emergency and with prior permission from the police or security forces. People travelling for an emergency would be required to produce their national identity cards and other relevant documents to security personnel.

Residents have been directed to follow the instructions of security personnel during the curfew.

Meanwhile, Upper South Waziristan DC Irfan Ali said Section 144 would remain in force in the Sarwekai and Ladha tehsils of Upper South Waziristan from 6am to 7pm on Monday.

All kinds of movement would remain restricted in the notified areas, while markets and business centres would remain closed during the period.

Several major routes in Upper South Waziristan have also been declared out of bounds. These include the route from Ladha through Makeen, Tabai Sar, Bibi Raghzai, Kotkai and Spinkai Raghzai to Nazar Khel.

The route from Dargai Bridge through Medi Jan, Sheen Warsak, Mola Khan Sarai and Chagmalai to Jandola has also been included in the restrictions.

Similarly, the route from Sarwekai through Mola Khan Sarai to Barwand will remain closed to general traffic during the notified period.

The Upper South Waziristan administration said only emergency movement would be permitted on the affected roads and that travellers would have to obtain permission from the police or security forces.

In Tank district, DC Jamshed Khan said Section 144 would be enforced in Jandola subdivision from 6am to 7pm on Monday.

The restrictions would cover Jandola bazaar and other notified areas, where all business centres would remain closed and general movement would be prohibited during the specified hours.

According to the notification issued by the Tank administration, the route from Kour fort through Khargai to Jandola and up to the boundary between Tank district and Upper South Waziristan would remain closed. Jandola bazaar has also been included in the restricted area.

Another affected route runs from Dabra through Kour fort, Gardavi, Gomal Zam Dam and Gulgi Kot to Dabra and up to the boundary between Tank district and Lower South Waziristan. Kor bazaar has also been included in the restrictions.

The three district administrations have appealed to residents, traders, transporters and travellers to avoid unnecessary movement during the specified hours and remain at home unless there is an unavoidable emergency.

The restrictions are expected to affect movement between the three districts, which are geographically connected through several major roads and link routes. The authorities have therefore included some inter-district routes in the notifications to regulate movement during the specified period.

Residents have been urged to plan their travel accordingly and avoid the affected routes on August 10 to prevent inconvenience.

The district administrations of Upper and Lower South Waziristan had also imposed Section 144 in several areas in June due to security concerns and the movement of security forces.

South Waziristan, as well as the rest of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, has been facing terrorism for a long time.

According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026.

World.title: Houthi attacks kill 11 in Yemen, target Saudi oil refinery
World.content:
Strikes by Houthi rebels on Sunday killed at least 11 people, a medical source in the Yemeni port city of Mokha told AFP, after an earlier drone salvo targeted a Saudi oil refinery on the Red Sea coast.

A years-long truce in Yemen’s civil war between the Houthis and the internationally recognised government appeared to collapse last month as fighting between regional allies of the United States and Iran flared.

The breakdown of the UN-backed 2022 accord came as the rebels announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, hitting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and the kingdom’s oil infrastructure, in parallel with Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

A medical source in Mokha, held by Yemen’s internationally recognised, Aden-based government, said three civilians and eight military personnel had been killed in the Houthi attacks.

A further 32 individuals were wounded, six of them civilians, the source added, explaining all the civilian casualties had been a result of strikes on Mokha’s port.

Two military sources with the government forces earlier confirmed at least eight troops had been killed in the strikes and more than 40 personnel were injured.

The Houthis’ military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the group had targeted “Saudi enemy” troops and equipment in the area with missiles and drones.

The two military sources with the Aden-based government confirmed the Houthis attacked Yemen’s Mokha with several waves of missile and drone barrages.

One of the two military sources said the Houthis also targeted pro-government forces and installations outside Mokha and sites on islands near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

The same military source said some locations targeted by Houthis housed Saudi troops but no casualties had been reported among military personnel from the Gulf kingdom.

Residents in government-controlled Mokha confirmed to AFP they heard blasts in the area, with one saying they “heard explosions from drones and air defences over the port and city”.

Another resident said they heard “six consecutive explosions” in the port.

Aramco oil facility targeted

Earlier in the day, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said civil response teams had brought under control a fire at the Jazan refinery, without giving the cause of the blaze.

“Saudi Aramco’s industrial security firefighting teams extinguished a fire that broke out at dawn today, Sunday, at one of the facilities belonging to the Saudi Aramco refinery in Jazan, without any injuries,” the ministry said.

Saree claimed that Houthis attacked the facility operated by Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil firm in response to incursions by drones from the kingdom into northwest Yemen.

The facility was also targeted by Yemen’s Houthi rebels in July. Aramco had shut down the refinery as the attack damaged the plant’s Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) complex and tank farm area, according to a note from consultancy IIR seen by Reuters.

The Jazan refinery processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day and produces refined products including gasoline and ultra-light sulfur diesel.

Aramco chief Amin Nasser said last week that recent attacks on the company’s facilities had caused some production interruptions but that he was confident operations could be restored quickly. He said the attacks had no material operational or financial impact.

The Houthis control vast swathes of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and areas on the border with Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea provinces.

The Yemeni threat to shipping and Saudi oil facilities comes in parallel with Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which has become the central flashpoint between Tehran and Washington amid efforts to end the Middle East war begun by the US and Israel in February.

In July, the Houthis had announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, hitting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea.

Pakistan had condemned the Houthis’ threats to Saudi Arabia and to trading with the kingdom via the Red Sea. It also warned that it had the right to self-defence if its “maritime interests” were targeted in “any hostile act”.

Last week, Saudi Arabia unveiled plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition to protect shipping and energy supply routes in the Red Sea. Fourteen countries, including Pakistan, have voiced support for the coalition.

On Friday, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed a joint defence agreement under which an attack against one of them would be treated as an attack against all of them.

World.title: Lionel Messi bids farewell to father who guided his glittering career
World.content:
Argentina football icon Lionel Messi bid farewell on Sunday to his father, the global star’s emotional anchor and agent since childhood, who passed away following a battle with cancer aged 68.

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner touched down on a private flight from Miami late on Saturday with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and their children and has remained surrounded by his close family since.

A private ceremony with a few teammates from the Argentine national squad is scheduled to take place at a cemetery in the town of Perez, adjacent to Rosario, later Sunday.

The gates of the town’s El Prado cemetery displayed handwritten messages from fans — “Stay strong, Leo, we love you” and “Stay strong, Messi family” — alongside a large floral wreath.

Messi’s teammates rallied around their captain following the announcement that Jorge Messi had passed away late on Friday at a clinic in Rosario.

“It will surely do him good for us to be there,” Boca Juniors midfielder Leandro Paredes told journalists after his team’s match on Saturday.

“I need to speak with a few of my teammates to see if we go now or sometime tomorrow.”

According to some media outlets, midfielder Rodrigo de Paul — a close friend of Messi and his Inter Miami teammate — would travel to Argentina.

After scoring a goal in a 2-1 defeat to Monterrey in Miami on Saturday, De Paul paid tribute to his friend by taking off his shirt to reveal Messi’s number 10 jersey.

The cause of death was not disclosed, but local media reported that Jorge Messi had been suffering from cancer.

His unusual absence from the World Cup in June had already attracted attention.

Messi’s family asked the media for “humanity” during the tournament amid persistent rumours over Jorge’s health.

After bursting into tears after scoring against Algeria, 39-year-old Messi had admitted to dealing with “a situation outside of sports”.

“I went through a few difficult, complicated days,” he later acknowledged, “but I am grateful to the entire delegation and my teammates, because they stood by me, as always.”

Immediately after the World Cup final defeat against Spain, Messi returned to spend a few days with his family in Rosario.

Humble beginnings

A guiding figure throughout his son’s career, Jorge Messi was his first coach, who left everything behind to accompany his son to Spain.

A metalworker in Rosario, 340 km north of Buenos Aires, Jorge managed youth teams at the small local club Grandoli.

He was the one who introduced Argentina’s future captain to the game aged four on vacant lots where local kids played.

His life changed course in 2000 when Barcelona invited the young prodigy, then aged 13, to Catalonia to continue treatment for a growth hormone deficiency while playing for the club’s youth teams.

Jorge left behind his job in Argentina, his wife, and his three other children to settle in Spain with Lionel.

“When we arrived in Barcelona, I used to lock myself in my room to cry alone, and my father did the same — either without me seeing him or thinking I didn’t see him. We pretended we were both fine, but we were struggling,” Messi later said.

His father was later the agent who negotiated astronomical contracts on his behalf, from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami.

Messages of sympathy have poured in since Saturday from the football world, including from the clubs Messi played for and the Spanish Football Federation.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) ordered a minute of silence before matches and that black armbands be worn at games across all age groups for the week.

World.title: Pakistan rejects Afghan Taliban claims of weapons smuggled into Afghanistan as 'frivolous, baseless'
World.content:
The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on Sunday rubbished claims made by the Afghan Taliban about weapons allegedly smuggled from Pakistan into Afghanistan as “frivolous” and “baseless”.

In a statement shared on X, the ministry said, “The Afghan Taliban regime’s claim that weapons are being smuggled from Pakistan into Afghanistan for so-called ‘subversive activities’ is frivolous, baseless and contrary to established facts.”

It noted that Afghanistan was already awash with “enormous quantities of sophisticated weapons and military equipment abandoned after the withdrawal of US and coalition forces (worth an estimated $7.2 billion), in addition to large stocks of Soviet-era weaponry accumulated over decades of conflict”.

“Attempts to manufacture a Pakistani connection to such weapons seem designed to divert international attention from the far more serious and documented concern[s]: terrorist groups continue to find space, facilitation and operational freedom on Afghan soil to plan, support and execute attacks inside Pakistan,” the ministry stated.

It added that rather than resorting to “implausible accusations and blame-shifting”, the Afghan Taliban must address the “presence of terrorist sanctuaries on their territory and fulfil their repeated commitments that Afghan soil will not be allowed to be used for terrorism against Pakistan or any other country”.

Pakistan has been continuously pushing the Afghan Taliban regime to rein in the terrorist hideouts in Afghanistan and prevent the violent groups from carrying out terror activities against Pakistan from its soil. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

Last month, following multiple major attacks in Balochistan, Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir had asserted that terrorism originating from across the border would be crushed with the “full might of the state”.

In November 2025, Pakistan warned at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) that the acquisition of abandoned weapons by terrorist groups based in Afghanistan not only threatens peace and security in Pakistan but also in the region.

In April that year, an investigation by The Washington Post revealed that terrorists who attacked the Jaffar Express train in Balochistan used weapons left behind when United States forces withdrew from Afghanistan.

World.title: Curfew imposed in Balochistan Surab's district over law and order concerns
World.content:
QUETTA: The district administration of Surab on Sunday imposed a curfew across the district till August 15, citing concerns over the law and order situation.

According to an official notification, “The curfew will remain in force daily from 8pm to 9am during the specified period, starting from August 9 to 15, 2026.”

The administration also directed citizens to avoid leaving their homes unnecessarily during curfew hours, fully cooperate with law enforcement agencies, and strictly follow the security standard operating procedures (SOPs) issued for the protection of their families.

The notification warned that individuals violating the curfew would be responsible for any harm or loss resulting from their actions.

Legal action would be taken against those found violating the restrictions, it added.

Revised timings for Khuzdar commercial centres

Meanwhile, the district administration of Khuzdar announced revised operating hours for commercial centres across the district amid growing security concerns.

According to a notification issued by the office of the Khuzdar deputy commissioner, the measure had been taken temporarily as a precaution to protect the lives and property of citizens and the business community.

Under the new order, all markets, shops, hotels and other commercial establishments in Khuzdar district will remain closed from 8pm to 10am daily.

The order will be effective immediately and will remain in force until further directives.

However, pharmacies, medical stores, private hospitals and other healthcare facilities have been exempted from the restriction because of the essential nature of their services.

The district administration directed assistant commissioners, magistrates and police officials to ensure strict implementation of the order in their respective areas.

The administration also urged traders and the public to cooperate with the authorities to help minimise potential security threats and ensure the safety of citizens and their property.

Officials said the restrictions would be reviewed and amended only after an assessment of the security situation.

Earlier this week, the district authorities in Kalat and Khuzdar directed traders and the business community to close shops in the evening and advised residents to remain indoors at night due to security concerns.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels.
