World.title: Auckland fog forces flight cancellations, delays
World.content:
A spokesperson for Auckland Airport says some regional and domestic flights will be effected after a morning of disruptions.

Eight domestic flights were cancelled and a further six delayed - including five international - as a result of thick fog.

The fog was visible over the harbour early on Monday, with a band of fog lying over Auckland's North Shore.

There was further disruption after a fire alarm evacuation at the airport.

Travellers were re-entering the domestic terminal after emergency services completed necessary checks.

World.title: Ohakune's water shutdown likely to last longer than expected
World.content:
Ohakune's pipeline problem is more serious than originally thought, with the mayor unable to confirm when the town will have water again.

Water supplies to the central North Island town were turned off after last month's earthquake near Taumarunui likely damaged a major water pipeline.

The town's water reservoir is down to 12 percent.

Ohakune faces water shutdown Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Ruapehu District Mayor Weston Kirton told Morning Report it had been more difficult to fix the piping than had been initially thought.

"We've found the leak, we've actually fixed the leak, we've then tried to flush the system out and it's not working that well... and so we're obviously working hard to overcome that problem."

There was about 5km of concrete piping that was about 70 years old and may have been affected by the earthquake, he said.

But it was in difficult-to-access terrain which was hard to flush out, he said.

"As soon as we get on top of the airlocks then we'll be able to manufacture the water and then open the systems up for the town, but it's certainly concerning."

The water had been expected to be back on by Monday afternoon, but Kirton said that was no longer the case, and he did not want to speculate on when it would be back on.

Weston Kirton says it will take longer than initially expected to get the town's regular water system fixed. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The water plant was brand new and the issue was actually getting the water to the plant, he said.

The emergency situation was worsening and they would be dealing with that this morning, Kirton said.

"It could well be that we have an emergency situation to actually get water from elsewhere, through tankers or the like."

It would take longer than expected to get the existing plant up and running, he said.

It may be necessary to put an emergency water system in place before Ohakune's regular system can be fixed, he said.

"So I can't speculate whether it's a state of emergency yet, but that's one of the considerations you know whether we call on the government for help to actually overcome the issue with our town."

There was an influx of people in Ohakune at this time of year and there were businesses that wanted to be open and operating, he said.

"So we've got to have a Plan B and we'll take whatever measure it takes to make sure we actually get water to the households."

Currently there are emergency porta-loos around the town and water tankers which could be used in emergency situations, he said. They were setting up a centre at the Ruapehu District Council where people could come and collect as much water as they liked.

World.title: Carlton fans chant 'we want Fraser', talks on coaching future imminent
World.content:
Carlton fans are chanting Josh Fraser's name and a similar endorsement from the club's hierarchy for the Blues' interim coach to take the reins full time could follow as soon as this week.

Fraser has mounted an irrepressible case to take on the vacant head coach role, having delivered 10 wins and just two losses since stepping up when Michael Voss was sacked in mid-May, with the Blues at 1-8.

The interim coach, who earned "we want Fraser" chants from Carlton fans after last night's 44-point win, is yet to officially throw his hat in the ring — but that conversation is imminent.

Loading...

"At some stage this week there'll be an opportunity to have some conversations with the club," Fraser said.

"It'll be sometime this week."

Half-back Adam Cerra joked whether the interim boss taking the reins was the hardest question at the club at the moment.

"Obviously the club's got their processes. We've got full faith in that process and their decision and we'll support whatever they pick. 'Frase' has been great," he said.

"The boys obviously love playing with him. We'll leave that to the club."

Cerra put Carlton's turnaround down to a combination of Fraser's influence and how the playing group lifted him — with experienced players leading from the front and young players expressing themselves.

"Frase has probably allowed a bit of freedom for us to do that, a bit of simplicity in the way we're trying to play," Cerra said.

"It hasn't set too many boundaries on us. It's more trying to explore what our best football looks like and building that week to week.

"These last couple of weeks we've been getting more confidence in our process and our trust and executing."

Fraser was asked whether part of his thinking in holding off on nominating was around managing if he missed out on the job while preparing the team for a potential wildcard match.

Blues plant one foot in the AFL finals as Saints lose star to hamstring Carlton plants one foot in the AFL finals series with a statement victory over the Saints at Docklands.

"It's a fair question, but no, I haven't thought too deeply about that," the 43-year-old said.

"I've just tried to stay as narrow as I can and it's been challenging with a lot of the questioning and different things, but I still feel such a responsibility to this role as interim coach.

"That's what I needed to, and have, focused all of my energy on — because I would be doing a disservice, not only to our players, but our staff and everyone, if I started to stray away from that.

"Clearly I've had to think through some things, but that hasn't occupied a lot of my thinking and all the hypotheticals haven't either. Most of my energy has been focused on this playing group and footy club."

The Blues sit eight points clear in 10th with games against the Western Bulldogs and Fremantle to come.

"[It's] not about daring to dream, I think the thing that's taking us forward is we are just attaching ourselves to the work that we need to do," Fraser said.

AAP

World.title: 'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open
World.content:
Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner has pulled out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

The 24-year-old, who claimed his fifth grand slam title at Wimbledon last month, had also pulled out of the Canadian Open, a key warm-up event for the US Open at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Sinner won the Cincinnati title in 2024 and finished runner-up to seven-times grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz there last year.​‌

"After consulting with my doctors and my team, I have to announce that I need to withdraw from the Masters 1000 tournament in Cincinnati," Sinner said in a statement.

"My right knee has been bothering me and even though we have been working hard with my medical team, I have to accept that I'm not ready to compete yet.

"I'm very disappointed not to be able to play in Cincinnati … I can't wait to be back next year and I'm now focusing on getting ready for the U.S. Open."

Sinner's withdrawal further depletes the field in Cincinnati, with US Open champion Alcaraz also sidelined by a wrist injury.

The Cincinnati Open main draw begins on August 13, while the US Open main draw gets underway on August 30.

Reuters

World.title: 'Go chase the dreams': Vollering wins second Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
After winning the Tour de France Femmes for the second time on Sunday, Demi Vollering tried hard to hold back tears while the Dutch national anthem played.

It was her toughest moment of the day after an ultra-dominant performance on the bike from the 2023 champion.

She secured an impressive stage win, and in doing so extended her overall lead to 1 minute, 18 seconds over 2024 champion Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney, from Poland.

Vollering raised her bike in the air moments after crossing the finish line in Nice. Niewiadoma-Phinney had started Sunday's ninth and final stage only eight seconds behind Vollering, who got a time bonus for winning it.

Finally, as the Dutch anthem ended, a lone tear trickled down the side of Vollering's face. A few more soon followed as her achievement hit home.

"It's not only the dream of winning the Tour de France. It's also the dream of living this life, of working hard along with passionate people," the 29-year-old Vollering said.

"It all starts with dreaming. Go chase the dreams and don't let anyone stop you."

Nobody could on Sunday.

Knowing that she was well clear, Vollering began to celebrate as the line approached, raising her arm in triumph and then tapping her head with her finger to show her mental strength.

"I was thinking about a lot of things as I was approaching the finish line. I thought that I had never won in the yellow jersey before," Vollering said. "I thought about how much work has gone into this victory. I thought about the people who have been behind me."

She finished the stage 1 minute, 4 seconds ahead of Spaniard Paula Blasi Cairol and Niewiadoma-Phinney, who looked tired but was all smiles later on the podium.

Former Giro d'Italia champion Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy was third overall in the Tour — 4:29 behind — after Marlen Reusser lost valuable time after crashing going downhill after the second of the day's four climbs.

Reusser ended up 14th overall at nearly 26 minutes behind.

Niewiadoma-Phinney had it all to do on the final climb, especially with her rival sitting on her wheel, and was unable to pressure Vollering.

Vollering attacked about 800 meters from the top and dropped Niewiadoma-Phinney — as she did when winning Saturday's eighth stage to take the overall lead from her rival.

Two years ago, Vollering missed out on Tour victory after finishing an agonising four seconds behind Niewiadoma-Phinney on the last stage.

She made full amends this time.

Vollering has now won five Grand Tours, including two Spanish Vuelta titles and the Giro d'Italia secured in June to join countrywoman Annemiek van Vleuten as the only other female cyclist to have won all three Grand Tours.

"I still have a lot of dreams," Vollering said. "On and off the bike."

Each of the first three climbs on Sunday was 7.7 kilometres long with a 5.9 per cent average gradient. But the final ascent branched off onto a slightly different route which, even though it was shorter at 6 kilometres, had a steeper average gradient of 7.6 per cent with one portion stretching to a gruelling 12 per cent.

It made little difference.

After winning Friday's seventh stage with an impressive solo attack of her own up the iconic Mont Ventoux, Niewiadoma-Phinney seemed short of energy, and Vollering's lead was never under threat.

AP

World.title: 'Licence to play': New Wallabies coach backing players in attack
World.content:
The Wallabies are committing to having a crack after being given a "licence to play" by new coach Les Kiss, having avoided an Osaka disaster.

Australia defied a 20-minute red card and brutal heat and humidity to pip Eddie Jones's plucky Japan 35-32 and ensure the Kiss era began with victory on Saturday.

Fly half Declan Meredith battled all night to make ground with his exit kicks, and the fluency shown in a last-start flogging of Italy was not there.

Wallabies survive scare as Kiss era begins with win New Wallabies coach Les Kiss says his side will need to learn how to control their ambitions after Australia hangs on to win a frantic Test match against Japan in the Osaka heat.

But, after winning just five of 15 Tests under Joe Schmidt last year, the Wallabies did enough and will meet Japan again in friendlier conditions in Townsville this Saturday afternoon, hoping to find a higher gear.

"We've tweaked a few things, but we didn't even really get to see those out there," halfback Ryan Lonergan said.

Japan's opening try came after Fraser McReight had won a turnover and raced out of his own 22-metre area with a quick tap, only to turn the ball over with a speculative pass.

When the Wallabies were clinging to a late lead, Meredith also fumbled a quick tap directly in front of Japan's posts that handed back possession.

"He (Kiss) has given us the licence to play and is all for us having a crack … (If we) see space, take it," Lonergan said.

"Now it's up to us to know how to make use of it … we've got to know that when we take that space we've got to be on board with it and commit."

Kiss made four changes to the starting side in his first Test since taking over from Schmidt, and said more were inevitable in Townsville.

Lock Miles Amatosero's red card will likely see him suspended — Lukhan Salakaia-Loto was firming for a Townsville return anyway — while the forward pack could be shuffled further, with prop Isaac Kailea unused in Japan after his recall to the squad.

Called in as injury cover, young prop Massimo De Lutiis could become Wallaby number 1,000 in Townsville.

Australia's 999th Wallaby on his injury-riddled road to Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

How Kiss responds to Meredith's middling night, particularly with the boot in general play, will be crucial given Carter Gordon is fit for a return.

"I'd imagine there will be one or two tweaks," Kiss said.

"This trip took a lot out of a lot of guys; we'll have to look at where the energy is, and at the numbers, because you lose a lot of weight."

Kiss acknowledged his side's kicking struggles, that they had overplayed or been impatient and struggled to defend around the ruck.

But the coach's composure in the box rubbed off, cameras catching him laughing late in the game with the result in the balance.

"It wasn't frivolous," Kiss said of the coaching booth gag.

"We're learning about each other in the box, getting on well, and it was a nice little moment; I know it was tight, but you've got to have fun doing this, too."

Kiss, the former Kangaroos and Queensland rugby league winger, has pushed an Australia brand to his playing style, likening the mentality to backyard footy and cricket battles.

"It's a balance of backing yourself and managing the game at the right time," he said.

"I just ask us to be skilful, and the nature of the game at times probably said 'let's just hold it a bit'.

"We had to come up with quality when shit happened, and we did that."

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the second Test match between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday, August 15.

AAP

World.title: NRL clubs split on playing Alameddine brothers over gang war concerns
World.content:
Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs is allowing a promising young player in its ranks to continue playing despite his brother being benched over concerns for his safety due to familial links to Sydney's Alameddine crime family.

Bulldogs five-eighth Zain Alameddine ran out in the blue and white on Saturday in the Ron Massey Cup despite his brother, Parramatta Eels young gun Mohamed, being sidelined as a result of the city's escalating gang war.

The ABC can reveal the Bulldogs have been in extensive contact with the NRL Integrity Unit over Zain Alameddine's personal safety and ability to play.

The club has taken a series of measures to protect his safety, including providing security, who liaise directly with police at games he plays in.

The promising Bulldogs number seven only recently moved from Parramatta Eels himself. (Supplied)

The NRL's Integrity Unit has been working with NSW Police and providing advice to the Bulldogs on the matter, and has also done so for Parramatta.

The ABC understands that there is no immediate threat to Zain's safety and, as a result, Canterbury-Bankstown has opted to continue playing him, unlike Parramatta.

The Ron Massey Cup is the third-tier competition of semi-professional rugby league in New South Wales, while the NSW Cup is the highest level of competition and is one grade below the NRL, the professional competition.

Zain Alameddine has played predominantly in the Ron Massey Cup after playing earlier this year in the junior rugby league tournament, the SG Ball Cup.

Both Zain and Mohamed Alameddine are not accused of any wrongdoing, any involvement in organised crime, or the crime family bearing their last name.

Mohamed Alameddine is a development player for the Parramatta Eels.

The Alameddines operate a crime network out of Sydney's western suburbs, but its senior figures remain in hiding in Lebanon after fleeing the country in 2023.

Police believe a series of shootings and arson attacks over the past six months are linked to its feud with the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel", which takes its name from a historic slur against Pasifika people.

The decisions by the Bulldogs and the Eels come after a series of attacks between the two gangs spilling into public life.

One involved a foiled plot to kill an alleged member of the Alameddines at a suburban rugby league match in April.

The intended target, Ali Younes, was watching a game at Ringrose Park next to the Wenty Leagues Club when his alleged would-be assassins were spotted nearby and fled.

The ABC understands he was watching another Alameddine family member play.

Police intercepted that car and arrested three men at Homebush after pinning it along the M4 motorway, seizing a long-arm rifle and a pistol.

Three men were arrested and firearms seized after a car fled a suburban footy ground in April. (ABC News)

Police said during their pursuit of the car the three men inside allegedly threw jerry cans and bleach out of the window.

The car, police said, had been linked to a number of shootings before the Wentworthville plot.

Another incident in June saw a relative of the Alameddines and a young girl escape unharmed after a hitman's gun jammed in an attempted gangland assassination during a school pick-up in Fairfield.

New South Wales Rugby League has also been monitoring the situation and is in regular communication with both clubs; ultimately, decisions on who to select for the club remain with the club in both instances.

Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs did not respond to requests for comment, including why they have taken a different decision to Parramatta.

The ABC understands the club has worked closely to ensure Zain Alameddine can play safely and pursue his sporting dream.

The NRL, Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs and the NSWRL have all been contacted for comment.

World.title: Blues start AFLW season with 26-point win over Saints
World.content:
Carlton has held off a St Kilda fightback to claim the opening win of the new AFLW season by 26 points in an entertaining game that made a case for more double header fixtures.

The Blues made the preliminary final last season and entered 2026 with high expectations.

Carlton led by as much as 31 points but withstood a fourth-quarter comeback from St Kilda before sealing the 9.12 (66) to 6.4 (40) victory.

Loading Instagram content

Sunday's game was held at Docklands Stadium ahead of the men's AFL clash as one of five double headers this season.

The concept already appears a winner and will prompt calls for more alignment with the men's season.

Several thousand fans were in for the start of the game, with the crowd ticking over 10,000 just after half-time and reaching 20,455 when the attendance was officially counted in the fourth quarter.

Despite missing young dynamo Sophie McKay (calf), best and fairest winner Keeley Sherar (quad) and ruck recruit Lauren Bella (calf) through injury, the Blues were on top early.

The Saints couldn't capitalise on early centre clearance dominance and were swamped by Carlton's classy midfield.

Skipper Abbie McKay (32 disposals, nine clearances), Mimi Hill (28 disposals), Lila Keck (21 disposals, two goals) recruit Claudia Whitfort (27 touches) and Irish star Dayna Finn (22 disposals) collected plenty of the ball, while Lily Goss kicked two goals.

Young gun Poppy Scholz was the fire starter, brushing off a defender to kick the first goal, kicking 1.4 and appearing a constant threat with her athleticism and smarts.

Scholz's opener started a run of four straight Carlton goals.

Tyanna Smith was comfortably St Kilda's best, racking up 625 metres gained, eight clearances, 19 disposals and two terrific goals on the run, with support from Georgia Patrikios (27 disposals)

Amber Clarke provided a spark with two superb fourth-quarter goals.

Overwhelmed by Carlton's running power early, the Saints got a foothold in the game when recruit Sophie Butterworth nailed their first goal.

St Kilda smashed Carlton around the ball in the third term and cut the deficit to 23 at three-quarter time.

Clarke soccered through a wonderful skidding goal from a tight angle to spark St Kilda just 27 seconds into the final term, then snapped another to cut the lead to 11.

But Darcy Vescio's second goal put a dagger in St Kilda's hearts late on before Keck sealed the deal.

St Kilda's J'Noemi Anderson suffered a hamstring injury.

Mathew Buck's Carlton next host Adelaide at Princes Park while Nick Dal Santo's St Kilda travel to Geelong.

AAP

World.title: Munster free to play after dangerous contact charge downgraded
World.content:
Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster has avoided suspension after the NRL Match Review Committee downgraded his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

Munster was initially facing a week on the sidelines, and two if he unsuccessfully challenged the charge, for a low tackle at the knees of Sea Eagles prop Taniela Paseka.

The Storm star was the third man in to the tackle, targeted the legs of Paseka, and left the Manly big man in pain.

Paseka was helped from the field, and Munster was charged with a grade two dangerous contact.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

But the MRC has now downgraded that to a grade one, after receiving a medical report that shows Paseka's injury may not be as bad as first feared.

A statement from the NRL says new information warranted the charge being downgraded, which means Munster can cop a $750 fine for pleading guilty.

"When initially ascribing a grading to Melbourne Storm's Cameron Munster for the charge of dangerous contact, the MRC considered the contents of a medical report provided by the injured player’s club, which offered preliminary details as to the nature and extent of the injury," the NRL statement said.

"Subsequently, the match review committee has received a further report which materially alters the nature and extent of the injury suffered by the player.

"Pursuant to Rule 61 of the NRL Judiciary Code, where further expert or medical information warrants a different grading, the match review committee may authorise the match review manager to amend the grading and issue an amended notice of charge.

"Following due consideration of this report, the match review committee has reviewed the charge against Cameron Munster and, in accordance with the judiciary code, has forwarded the player an amended notice of charge for the offence of dangerous contact (grade 1)."

Munster made his return to action following a knee injury in the Storm's win over the Sea Eagles in Perth, keeping alive their very slim finals hopes.

The Storm have the bye next week, then must win their remaining three matches starting with a clash against Penrith at AAMI Park.

Even if the Storm win their remaining three matches, they will need other results to go their way.

World.title: Rising Aussie UFC star calls for tougher fighters after first-round win
World.content:
The moment was not too big for Quillan Salkilld.

Making his main event debut, the Australian's run of first-round finishes continued on Saturday night local time in Las Vegas as he defeated veteran Mateusz Gamrot with a rear-naked choke at 4:25 of the first round of their non-title lightweight bout at UFC Fight Night at the UFC APEX.

Salkilld (13-1) survived a Gamrot (26-5) leg-lock during an extensive grappling exchange in the scheduled five-round fight before working to the back and locking in the finish, earning the biggest victory of his career while extending his winning streak to 13 fights.

Salkilld, who has now won his past four fights and five of his last six in the first round, called for a step up in competition after the victory.

"I think I deserve someone who's in the top five or close to it," Salkilld said.

Following the victory, the number 12-ranked Salkilld positioned himself for a match-up near the top of the lightweight division, while the number eight-ranked Gamrot absorbed a setback against one of the division's fastest-rising contenders.

Saturday's event marked the UFC's return to Las Vegas after two events abroad, in Abu Dhabi on July 25 and then Belgrade last Saturday.

In the co-main event, Diego Ferreira (20-7 MMA) landed more than 135 significant strikes across 15 minutes to earn a unanimous decision against Billy Quarantillo (18-8 MMA) in their lightweight bout.

All three judges scored the fight 30-27 for Ferreira, who kept Quarantillo on the defensive in Quarantillo's first Octagon appearance in more than 600 days after suffering a knee injury and his first lightweight fight since 2017.

Darren Elkins's UFC retirement fight ended unceremoniously as Yadier del Valle (11-1 MMA) needed one left hook to secure a TKO stoppage 35 seconds into the opening round of their featherweight bout.

Del Valle quickly closed the show against Elkins (29-13 MMA), spoiling the longtime veteran's final Octagon appearance while rebounding from the first loss of his career in February.

"I'm thankful for it all … don't ever give up on yourself," Elkins said following the loss.

Strawweight Alexia Thainara (15-1) utilised a relentless pace and a variety of take-downs alongside unorthodox striking to earn a unanimous decision against former strawweight contender Amanda Lemos (15-7-1), taking the cards 29-28, 29-28 and 30-27 in their all-Brazilian match-up.

Unbeaten welterweight Ty Miller (8-0 MMA) opened the main card by stopping Billy Ray Goff (9-5 MMA) via TKO 15 seconds into the third round.

Miller unleashed punches against the fence to force the stoppage, extending his perfect professional record while handing Goff his third straight defeat.

Reuters

Tech.title: No Dogs in Space is a music history podcast for true obsessives
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Sadly, there hasn’t been a new episode of No Dogs in Space since July of 2024. Part four of the podcast’s series on Can wrapped up an abbreviated season three, which focused on experimental rock. Don’t get me wrong, I loved seasons one and two, but the show seemed to be gearing up for a deep dive into Krautrock, and I was hype. Unfortunately, that episode ended with hosts Marcus Parks (Last Podcast on the Left) and Carolina Hidalgo declaring they were going to do another season on punk (the topic of season one), only for the feed to go quiet.

If you’re a music obsessive, this is a must-listen podcast. Over the course of 73 episodes, the husband-and-wife duo digs into the careers of the Beastie Boys, The Velvet Underground, Joy Division, and more. Even if you think you know everything there is to know about iconic bands like The Stooges, I guarantee there will be new info here.

The show dedicates multiple hours over the course of several episodes to its subjects. Its two-part intro to Krautrock, which heavily focuses on Amon Düül II is over three hours long, and that’s on the shorter side. The Replacements series is nearly nine hours long, and Beastie Boys is even longer still.

Over these exceptionally long series, it never gets dull, though. The two balance scripted info-dense sections with more improvisational sidebars expertly. They also, as you’d expect from a married couple, have great chemistry on mic. They also make sure to share all their sources at the end of the episode in case you want to track down the primary source or do your own fact-checking.

The show isn’t officially over. As recently as a couple of months ago, Carolina was responding to Instagram comments saying she’d love to do more episodes. And the possibility of the show returning has come up multiple times on live streams. But as of this writing, we’re still waiting on that Punk Rock 2.0 series.

Tech.title: Zuckerberg’s yacht was closer, but someone else saved a stranded boat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Earlier this week, the Alaskan cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued a small skiff stranded near Farragut Bay after running out of fuel. But, according to tracking data reviewed by the Alaska Beacon and Halifax Shipping News, the closest vessel was actually Mark Zuckerberg’s super yacht, Launchpad.

Michael Love, a passenger on the Wilderness Legacy, posted on Bluesky that the captain announced the Launchpad was closer, but “repeatedly refused to respond,” which was met with booing from the passengers. The AIS tracking (embedded below) seems to support that the Launchpad was closer to the vessel in trouble, but then stopped near the entrance of the bay. The Wilderness Legacy can be seen passing Launchpad, then turning around and towing the stranded boat back to safety.

The US Coast Guard and the Marine Exchange of Alaska did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But Coast Guard Public Affairs Specialist Shannon Shepard told the Alaska Beacon that “at approximately 9:56 p.m., the Coast Guard determined they were not in distress and issued a marine assistance request broadcast on their behalf.”

Brian Baker, spokesperson for Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, told The Verge that “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe.”

Tech.title: 49ers coach says his Tesla was on Autopilot when he crashed
Tech.content: “I’ve had Autopilot for nine years, so I’m pretty comfortable with it and, you know, who knows what happened when I turned around? Whether it malfunctioned or whether I knocked it off? That’s something I don’t know yet. But regardless, that’s… it is always your fault, whether you’re on Autopilot or not. You can’t take your eyes off the road. It’s a partnership driving, you don’t just turn it over to a computer.”

Tech.title: Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
Tech.content:
In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC — a scenario that would have left a lot of people very upset and placed me in deep trouble. I wasn’t irresponsible, I had local backups, but at some point I found myself in custody of so many important files that it scared me. And no matter how many redundancies I could build at home, they’d all still be in the same place — a risky bet. So I bought a subscription to Dropbox. Years later, it’s still one of the best software subscriptions that I happily renew each year.

It was great to have all that work backed up in the cloud — both for peace of mind and because it made working with collaborators breezier, letting them upload stuff directly to my drive, and letting me transfer files up to 50GB in size. In quick order I had built a trove of incredible artwork and complicated InDesign, Photoshop, and Illustrator files. The original goal for my Dropbox configuration was to make sure I wouldn’t lose any data in a worst-case scenario, so I set it up to mirror everything living on my work partition. Eventually, I ran smack into a worst-case scenario. Not once, but twice.

I’m still not sure why, but my latest home-built PC chewed through two separate 2TB Samsung 970 Evo SSDs. It’s difficult to tell what went wrong with them, but in each case I woke up one morning to find when I tried to boot up that no drive could be detected. I can still feel my stomach trying to sink into the floor when I press that power button these days, never knowing if my drive had died in its sleep.

Fortunately, both times, after some process-of-elimination testing I learned that just the drive had gone bad and everything else in my system was A-OK. Maybe I should have ditched Samsung after the second disaster, but I’m now on an 2TB 990 Evo Plus. Knock on wood, this thing better not fail. That drive now costs almost twice what I originally paid for it thanks to our new outrageously priced world of parts.

My Dropbox bill is about $204 a year for a family plan ($17 a month), which includes up to six members. If you’re just in it for yourself you can get it for $9.99 a month billed yearly (about $120 a year), which comes with 2TB of storage. You can upgrade to 3TB for around $143 a year. That might be a tough sell for people who already have dozens of subscriptions, but I find it to be a decent price for excellent digital insurance.

There are other powerful options out there, especially for professionals working with heavy files or complicated workflows. Backblaze, for example, has a personal backup plan with unlimited data for $99 a year and no restrictions on file size. And, of course, if you live on the Mac, Apple iCloud Plus isn’t a bad option — especially if you’re already paying for an Apple One subscription. Even Adobe offers file backups through Creative Cloud if that’s your jam, but I would not recommend using that clunky software suite for anything other than doing the work you need to do.

I can’t recall a single time the service failed

I prefer Dropbox because the software works consistently well across multiple operating systems and is usually neither seen nor heard. The Windows client is snappy and I’ve found with a fast internet connection that its real-time syncing is efficient and painless. Anytime a file is modified in the partition I have mirrored in the cloud, Dropbox quietly begins uploading it and making changes to my mirrored files in the cloud. After using it for about eight years now I can’t recall a single time the service failed or faltered. It’s so fast and reliable I often forget it’s even there.

Now, for the important caveat: This might not work for you if you have poor internet speeds. It really depends on how much data you’re regularly moving around on your computer and how quickly you make changes to it. This could particularly be a problem for asymmetrical data plans that commonly boast lightning-fast download speeds while offering pathetic upload speeds. I’ve done fine averaging only about 20Mbps upload, but if you’re on something even lower you should try a free trial for a backup plan before committing. You can also find plenty of download time calculators online; at my gigabit download speed it usually takes around two hours to download the 1TB of files I have synced in the cloud.

And one more caveat: Putting everything (or even just many things) on your computer in the cloud isn’t for everyone, and I completely understand why many folks wouldn’t or shouldn’t do that for sensitive files. I once built local RAID drives and even airgapped storage systems to avoid having everything online. These things are still possible but getting more expensive by the day as storage prices spike. You’re the best judge of how and where your data should be protected.

That sinking feeling of potentially losing my whole PC? It was immediately followed each time by the assurance that I’d only lost a computer’s body and not its soul. When I got my PC back up and running with new storage, it ended up taking less time to resync all my files than it did to troubleshoot and install new hardware. I can almost hear Billy Crudup doing a Mastercard commercial in my head: New solid state drive, three hundred eighty-nine dollars. Yearly Dropbox subscription, two hundred and three dollars. Never worrying about losing your data? Priceless.

Tech.title: AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more news about how AI is changing our daily lives, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Long before ChatGPT became a thing, educators and editors frequently used anti-plagiarism tools to see if writers were being honest about their work. These tools work by comparing a written work against a database filled with content from across the web, scholarly articles, and more to check for matching sentences and phrases. Some, like Turnitin, offer a percentage that claims to illustrate how much of the student’s writing overlaps with other works. Between potential false positives and uncertainty about whether work was duplicated intentionally, some educators have backed away from using that particular tool.

But now, the hunt for copied content is evolving into a war on AI-generated work. As quickly as students have picked up ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, teachers have adopted so-called AI detectors just as fast. A survey from the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 43 percent of sixth to 12th grade teachers in the US regularly used AI detectors between 2024 and 2025. Some universities already using Turnitin in their learning management systems found that the service automatically enabled AI detection when the tool launched in 2023.

Instead of comparing pieces of written content, AI detectors like GPTZero, Pangram, and the one created by Turnitin rely on their own AI models to guess whether something might not be human-written — a process that’s arguably even murkier than matching text on the web. As noted by GPTZero, AI detectors use an algorithm to analyze a text’s wording, rhythm, and structure, as well as to pick up on patterns in length and tone that may be more common in AI-written text. This relatively subjective evaluation isn’t as solid as something you could back up by matching text online, and can get tripped up by writers who speak English as a second language. Despite this, Turnitin has said that its AI detector falsely flags less than 1 percent of human-written content as AI, while Pangram claims its false positive rate is just 1 in 10,000. GPTZero claims it has a similarly low rate of mistaking human content for AI.

How it’s going

People online are already accusing each other of “sounding like AI,” but the ready availability of AI detection tools is only adding fuel to the LLM witch hunt. In some high-profile cases, AI writing accusations have directly impacted people’s livelihoods and reputations. Last month, the publisher Minotaur dropped a $2 million book deal over concerns that its author, Jerry Falade, used AI — something he vehemently denies.

There’s Thierry Rignol, a French national who sued Yale last year after a professor accused him of writing portions of his final exam with AI, resulting in a failing grade and a one-year suspension. The professor used GPTZero to scan Rignol’s writing for signs of AI, but the lawsuit argues that “AI surveillance and detection tools are known to unfairly target non-native English speakers” like Rignol. In February, a student at Adelphi University won a lawsuit against the school after his professor similarly claimed he used AI to write an essay. Though the lawsuit doesn’t say which AI tool the professor used to examine the student’s essay, Adelphi University has a licensing agreement with Turnitin.

As pointed out by the University of California, Los Angeles, AI detection tools are trained to pick up on patterns that could indicate AI use, such as repetitive terms and phrases, text that sounds too formal or informal, and nonsensical phrasing. Some, like QuillBot, also measure the “unpredictability” of text, as “AI tends to make the most ‘obvious’ or most common language choices as compared with human-produced writing,” according to UCLA. They may also look for sentence structure that remains the same throughout as another sign of AI. But these measurements aren’t indicative of AI on their own, as some people may just have a writing style with these qualities.

Even though Turnitin touts low false positive rates, it maintains that its tool “may not always be accurate” and shouldn’t be used to take actions against a student. Grammarly warns that users “should never rely on the results of an AI detector alone,” while GPTZero says “no AI detector can ever truly be 100% perfect.” OpenAI even shut down its own AI writing detector in 2023 due to low accuracy.

But AI writing accusations are still being flung across the web. Last week, in a video broadcast to the more than 3.5 million followers across his social channels, Ozzy Osbourne’s son, Jack, accused journalist and Verge contributor Kat Tenbarge of using AI to write an article for Rolling Stone, while flaunting the results from an AI detector, Getsolved, as “proof” of his claim. Tenbarge has refuted the claim in a video and a post on her website, but Osbourne hasn’t retracted his accusation or deleted the video, leaving Tenbarge to deal with the trolls.

There are numerous examples of false accusations, from writers to students, with many accusers failing to acknowledge the disclaimers that come along with some of these AI detection tools.

What happens next

The uncertainty surrounding AI detectors is enough for some educational institutions to stop using them altogether. Yale University, Johns Hopkins University, Vanderbilt University, Georgetown University, and others have disabled or restricted the use of AI detection tools. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology also warns that “AI detectors don’t work.”

Instead of relying on tools to weed out AI, many schools are encouraging educators to rethink their lessons. The University of Chicago, for example, suggests telling students to slow down their reading, breaking up longer writing assignments, and requiring students to reflect on their work. Stanford University says professors can consider holding assessments in classrooms, while MIT advises professors to leave room for students to disclose whether they used AI for help on an assignment, without penalty.

With AI becoming more prevalent in and outside the classroom, efforts to suss out what’s written by a human or a machine are ramping up as well. Some online platforms are only exacerbating suspicions surrounding AI use. Substack has built Pangram into its app, allowing users to scan blogs for suspected AI-generated content, while LinkedIn added a “seems like AI slop” button on posts. The result is a new era of distrust, where readers constantly question whether what they’re reading is AI and real human writers try their best not to sound like it.
